content_html:
1. Official currency: the Peruvian Sol
The country’s main currency is the Peruvian Sol (S/).

Basics:

  • It is the only officially accepted currency nationwide
  • It is divided into 100 cents
  • Common banknotes: 10, 20, 50, 100, and 200 soles
  • Coins: from 10 cents up to 5 soles

Tip: Always carry small change for minor purchases, especially in markets or public transport.

2. U.S. dollars: the second most used currency
The U.S. dollar is widely accepted in Peru, especially in tourism.

Where it’s used:

  • Hotels
  • Travel agencies
  • Tours and activities
  • Some large stores

Tip: Even though dollars are accepted, the exchange rate is often not favorable.

3. Exchange houses and exchange rates
Exchanging money is a key part of the experience.

Options:

  • Exchange houses (better rates)
  • Banks (safer, but lower rates)
  • Airport (least recommended due to high fees)

Tip: Compare exchange rates before converting large amounts of money.

4. Card payments and digital wallets
These are becoming increasingly common in Peru.

Accepted methods:

  • Debit and credit cards
  • Mobile apps like Yape and Plin

Tip: Carry cash, as not all places accept cards (especially outside major cities).

5. Common experiences (and how to handle them)

Many travelers go through this:

  • Not having small change
  • Receiving damaged bills (hard to use later)
  • Confusion about exchange rates

Solution: Always check your money and ask before paying in a different currency.

Tips for handling money in Peru

  • Avoid exchanging all your money at the airport
  • Use secure wallets or money belts
  • Don’t display large amounts of cash
  • Check bills before accepting them

Why understanding currency in Peru matters

Because it directly affects your experience:

  • Good money management = smarter purchases
  • Poor management = losses or unnecessary expenses

Knowing how money works gives you more control over your trip.
